title: Running Median of a Price Stream

statement.md: A market-data feed delivers trade prices one at a time. After every print you must report the *median* of every price seen so far. Trading systems do this constantly: the live median quote is used for spread monitoring, sanity checks on bad ticks, and solid reference prices that a single outlier print cannot drag around the way it drags a mean.

Recomputing the median from scratch after each price, sort everything, take the middle, costs $O(n \log n)$ per tick and $O(n^2 \log n)$ for the whole stream. A feed with hundreds of thousands of updates makes that unusable. You will maintain the median *incrementally* with two heaps.
Read a stream of n integer prices. After each price arrives, print the median of all prices seen so far, formatted with exactly one digit after the decimal point.

Median definition for a sorted list of k values: the single middle value if k is odd; the average of the two middle values if k is even. Since inputs are integers, every median is either an integer or a half-integer (x.0 or x.5), so one decimal digit is always exact, no rounding is ever needed.

statement.title: Why the median and not the mean?
statement.md: For price streams, the median is a solid location estimator: a fat-finger print of 0.01 or 100000 moves the mean a lot but leaves the median nearly untouched. Risk checks often compare the latest print against the running median rather than the running mean for exactly this reason.

inputFormat: Line 1: the integer n. Each of the next n lines contains a single integer price (one price per line, in arrival order).
outputFormat: Print n lines. Line i contains the median of the first i prices, formatted with exactly one digit after the decimal point (examples: 5.0, 4.5).
constraints: You must print exactly one output line per input price, in order.
hints: Keep the smaller half of the values in a max-heap and the larger half in a min-heap. Every value seen so far lives in exactly one of the two heaps.

Maintain the invariant that the lower heap has either the same number of elements as the upper heap or exactly one more. Then the median is the top of the lower heap (odd count) or the average of the two tops (even count).
After each insertion at most one element needs to move between the heaps to restore the invariant. Insert into the correct half first (compare with the top of the lower heap), then rebalance.

editorial.text: Approach: two heaps with a balance invariant

editorial.md: Split the values seen so far into a lower half L (the smallest ceil(k/2) values) held in a max-heap, and an upper half U (the rest) held in a min-heap, with the size invariant |L| = |U| or |L| = |U| + 1. Both heap tops are then the two middle order statistics, so the median is readable in O(1).

editorial.title: Per-price update
items: Let x be the new price. If L is empty or x <= top(L), push x onto L; otherwise push x onto U. This keeps every element of L <= every element of U.
Rebalance: if |L| > |U| + 1, pop the max of L and push it onto U. Otherwise if |U| > |L|, pop the min of U and push it onto L. Exactly one move happens at most.
Report: if |L| > |U| the median is top(L); otherwise it is (top(L) + top(U)) / 2.

editorial.md: Each insertion does O(1) heap pushes/pops, so the total cost is $O(n \log n)$ time and $O(n)$ memory. Reporting is O(1) per tick, which is the whole point: the per-tick latency no longer grows with the length of the stream.

All inputs are integers. An odd count gives a median equal to some input integer (an integer). An even count gives the average of two integers, which is either an integer or a half-integer. So printing with %.1f never faces a rounding decision beyond the exact .0 / .5 case. Compute the even-case average as an exact integer sum (it fits in 64 bits: at most 2*10^9) divided by 2.0.

editorial.title: Common bugs
editorial.md: 1) Rebalancing in the wrong direction (you must move from the bigger heap to the smaller one, and the invariant is that the LOWER heap may be one larger, never the upper). 2) Forgetting that the first value must go into the lower heap. 3) Summing the two heap tops in 32-bit arithmetic for the even case, 10^9 + 10^9 overflows 32-bit int.

solutions.python:
import heapq
import sys


def main():
    tok = sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()
    n = int(tok[0])
    low = []   # max-heap (negated): the smaller half
    high = []  # min-heap: the larger half
    out = []
    for s in tok[1:1 + n]:
        x = int(s)
        if not low or x <= -low[0]:
            heapq.heappush(low, -x)
        else:
            heapq.heappush(high, x)
        if len(low) > len(high) + 1:
            heapq.heappush(high, -heapq.heappop(low))
        elif len(high) > len(low):
            heapq.heappush(low, -heapq.heappop(high))
        total = -low[0] * 2 if len(low) > len(high) else -low[0] + high[0]
        out.append(f"{total // 2}.{5 if total % 2 else 0}")
    print('\n'.join(out))


main()
